title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
section: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text:
We introduce learned spectral codes, a compact linear representation that enables general spectral rendering through unmodified RGB pipelines. A trained encoder compresses any visible-range spectral quantity into a small latent vector; the codes are packed as RGB triplets and processed by an offthe-shelf RGB renderer. The codec preserves the arithmetic of light transport, exactly for scaling and addition and approximately for element-wise products, so two standard RGB passes suffice to produce results closely matching a full spectral rendering. The same codec handles reflectance, illumination, coloured glass, conductors, and participating media: one pipeline across material classes, with no per-material modification to the renderer.
Where spectral asset data is unavailable, lightweight neural upsamplers bridge legacy RGB inputs to the latent space. Across diverse materials and illumination, the method yields substantial quality improvements on the cases where RGB rendering fails most visibly, at rendering cost comparable to efficient spectral-sampling techniques and with no changes to the renderer.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text:
Spectral rendering propagates full spectral distributions through the rendering pipeline, reproducing wavelength-dependent phenomena that RGB rendering cannot: metamerism, prismatic dispersion, and thin-film interference [Watanabe et al . 2013]. Modern spectral renderers achieve this efficiently: hero wavelength sampling [Wilkie et al . 2014] and GPU-accelerated spectral path tracers [Murray et al . 2021] bring spectral rendering to near-RGB cost in open-source and custom production pipelines.
Much of the wider rendering ecosystem, however, remains RGBbased. Spectral pipelines such as Manuka [Fascione et al . 2018] exist in production, but commercial game engines, open-source suites such as Blender, GPU rasterisers, cloud render farms, and most proprietary offline renderers expose RGB inputs and RGB framebuffers only; modifying them to propagate stochastic wavelengths is impractical.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Recent work delivers individual spectral effects without touching the renderer core: Tominaga et al. [2026] render fluorescence through Mitsuba 0.6's spectral build by encoding the re-radiation into per-channel inputs, and Fichet et al. [2024] obtain a similar effect with a reduced re-radiation matrix implemented at the shader level. Fluorescence itself lies outside our supported regime, so these methods are complementary to ours.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Rendering general spectral content through multiple passes of an RGB pipeline originates with Darling et al. [2011], who relight scenes with a fixed six-channel parametric basis. We generalise this assets-only route, which requires no custom code anywhere: a single representation for per-channel-preserving spectral transport across reflectance, illumination, glass, conductors, and participating media, rendered through entirely unmodified RGB renderers. This representation, a learned spectral code, is a compact latent vector 𝑧 ∈ R 𝑘 that supports the per-channel arithmetic an RGB renderer already performs: scaling, addition, and element-wise multiplication. Spectral quantities encode into 𝑧; the codes pack into 𝑘/3 RGB triplets; the renderer processes them in 𝑘/3 unmodified passes; a final decode recovers the spectral radiance (Fig. 2 illustrates the full pipeline). Whether the renderer is Mitsuba, Blender Cycles, Maya Arnold, KeyShot, or a real-time rasteriser (Unreal Engine 5) is immaterial: each processes RGB triplets per channel, which is what the codec requires.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Exact preservation of all three operations is impossible whenever the code dimension 𝑘 is smaller than the number 𝑛 of spectral bins (Sec. 3.2), so the encoder is approximate by necessity. Our linear, non-negative architecture preserves scaling and addition exactly and is trained to approximate element-wise multiplication on the manifold of natural visible spectra. Since each RGB pass carries three channels, practical operating points are multiples of three; Sec. 6.1 establishes 𝑘=6 as the smallest configuration that is meaningfully more accurate than a standard RGB pipeline, with 𝑘=3 blocked by a Luther–Hadamard trade-off (alignment with the colour-matching subspace [Ives 1915; Luther 1927] against Hadamard preservation) and 𝑘=9 unwarranted in quality terms.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: The codec is content-agnostic: the same encoder–decoder embeds reflectance, illumination, transmittance, conductor IOR, and absorption and scattering coefficients into the same latent space (Sec. 4); two per-pixel upsamplers project legacy RGB assets onto the codec's manifold (Sec. 5). Our scope covers wavelength-preserving interactions; wavelength-shifting effects (fluorescence, dispersion) lie outside the supported regime (Sec. 7).

text: We evaluate the codec on broadband, narrowband, and multipeaked illumination across surface reflectance, coloured-glass transmission, conductor reflection, and homogeneous and heterogeneous subsurface scattering; the teaser (Fig. 1) exercises all of these in one scene. We benchmark timing and reconstruction quality against Mitsuba 3's hero wavelength sampling at matched resolution and spp, and we deploy the codec across four production renderers (Sec. 6).

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text:
Most compact spectral representations, ours included, are linear decompositions. Peercy [1993] introduced low-dimensional pointsampled representations for spectral rendering; PCA has been applied to reflectance and illumination datasets [Otsu et al . 2018] and to measured material capture [Guarnera et al . 2017; Matusik 2003]. PCA admits negative entries; NMF [Berry et al . 2007] is non-negative but needs more dimensions. Both serve as baselines in Sec. 6.1.
Parametric representations replace the data-fitted basis with a constrained family. Peters et al. [2019] encode bounded spectra as Fourier moments with a maximum-entropy reconstruction, achieving 3–8 coefficients with smooth, energy-conserving output. Karimipour et al. [2023] represent reflectance as 3×3 matrices fitted to cone responses, reaching Δ𝐸94 < 1 under broadband illumination but degrading to Δ𝐸94 up to 16 under narrowband sources. Both compress individual spectra accurately but provide no algebra on the compressed codes: the product of two compressed spectra cannot be evaluated without decompressing first.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Hero wavelength sampling [Wilkie et al . 2014] carries one stochastically chosen wavelength per ray with several stratified companions, reducing colour noise at near-RGB cost. West et al. [2020] generalise wavelength importance sampling to a continuous multiple importance sampling framework, and van de Ruit and Eisemann [2021] build coarse screen-space estimates over multiple passes to guide subsequent sampling. These methods improve efficiency within a spectral renderer; we target renderers with no spectral path at all.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Converting RGB textures to plausible spectra is a long-standing problem. Smits [1999] introduced a scaled basis-spectrum conversion with a long production history: the Manuka renderer relied on a Smits-style optimisation for all its uplifting [Fascione et al . 2018], and recent versions replace it with the moment-based method of Peters et al. [2019] for reflectances [Weidlich et al . 2021]. Meng et al. [2015] introduced a physically meaningful uplift over the XYZ space. Jakob and Hanika [2019] parameterise the sRGB gamut with three coefficients, smooth and energy-conserving; the method is now standard in PBRT-v4 [Pharr et al . 2023] and Mitsuba 3 [Jakob et al . 2022]. Jung et al. [2019] uplift gamuts wider than sRGB by adding fluorescent components. Belcour et al. [2023] give metameric one-to-many uplift for textured assets. Tódová et al.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: [2021; 2022] constrain the uplift so that selected spectra are reproduced exactly; Tódová and Wilkie [2025] extend uplifting to HDR environment maps, and van de Ruit and Eisemann [2024] constrain uplifted spectra by their rendered RGB appearance, including indirect illumination. Guarnera et al. [2022] target illumination spectra specifically, uplifting a light's tristimulus value by optimising blending weights over a compact spectral basis. They propose two variants: a measured basis of six LED primaries, which produces SPDs with the spectral structure of real multi-primary sources, and a smooth parametric Gaussian basis. Both reproduce the target chromaticity by construction; as with reflectance uplifting, the reconstructed SPD is one metamer of many, and the choice of basis decides which one. Xia et al. [2025] sample the null space of the RGB constraint via differentiable rendering. We benchmark our reflectance upsampler against Jakob and Hanika [2019] and our illumination upsampler against Guarnera et al. [2022] in Sec.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: A small but growing line of work delivers spectral phenomena without a spectral renderer. Ward and Eydelberg-Vileshin [2002] prefilter materials and lights before rendering, achieving near-exact direct illumination at the cost of approximate interreflection. Sun [2006] decomposes thin-film iridescence into a small number of RGB passes through an unmodified renderer. Fichet et al. [2024] handle fluorescence by replacing the albedo–light product with a reduced re-radiation matrix, requiring shader-level changes; their reducedmatrix formalism itself is general, and we adopt it in Sec. 3.4 to analyse our codec's constraints. Each of these methods is constructed for a specific phenomenon. We take a different route: a single learned codec supports general wavelength-preserving spectral transport (reflectance, illumination, coloured glass, conductors, and homogeneous and heterogeneous participating media) through any RGB renderer with no engine modification. Wavelength-shifting effects (fluorescence, phosphorescence, dispersion) couple distinct wavelengths during transport and remain outside the per-channel regime our codec preserves.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Fig. 2 summarises the system: a jointly trained encoder–decoder pair around otherwise unmodified RGB render passes. This section develops the constraints that shape it.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text:
Path tracing repeatedly applies three operations to spectral quantities: scaling (intensity, BSDF evaluation), addition (multiple light contributions, path accumulation), and element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication: reflectance with incident radiance, transmittance with through-flux, per-channel attenuation through participating media, and conductor Fresnel evaluated at the complex index 𝜂(𝜆)− 𝑖𝜅(𝜆) . 1 Discretising the visible spectrum on 𝑛 wavelength bins yields the algebra A = (R 𝑛 , + , ⊙) on which transport acts.
A renderer-friendly code must support the same three operations directly on the compact codes, so that the renderer can treat codes as ordinary 𝑘-channel inputs. Formally, this requires the encoder E to act as a ring homomorphism A → (R 𝑘 , + , ⊙) .
3.2 Impossibility of exact algebra-preserving compression
The compression we seek does not exist exactly:
Theorem 3.1. When 𝑘 < 𝑛 there is no injective ring homomorphism 𝜙 : (R 𝑛 , + , ⊙) → (R 𝑘 , + , ⊙) .

The argument is that the standard basis {𝑒1, . . . , 𝑒 𝑛 } forms a system of 𝑛 pairwise orthogonal nonzero idempotents under ⊙, while (R 𝑘 , + , ⊙) admits at most 𝑘 such idempotents [Atiyah and Macdonald 1969; Lang 2002], so for 𝑘 < 𝑛 at least one 𝑒𝑖lies in ker𝜙. The full proof and algebraic development are in Supplemental Sec. 1.
The natural relaxation is distributional preservation: scaling and addition are preserved exactly (a property our linear architecture below guarantees by construction), while Hadamard multiplication is preserved approximately on the low-dimensional manifold of natural visible spectra learned from data. The asymmetry is deliberate. Scaling and addition enter every radiance estimate through path accumulation and Monte-Carlo averaging, where a systematic error would bias the estimator itself; the Hadamard product enters once per material interaction, where a small approximation error is perceptually tolerable, and the multi-bounce measurements in Sec. 6.2 show that it does not accumulate.

Requiring (𝑅 𝑚 )𝑖𝑗 = 0 for all 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 and for every non-negative material spectrum 𝑚 forces each summand in Eq. (2) to vanish: 𝑊e 𝑊enc [𝑖, 𝜆]𝑊dec [𝜆, 𝑗] = 0 at every 𝜆, i.e. encoder row 𝑖 and decoder column 𝑗 must have disjoint supports for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗. Non-negativity is what makes this rigid: with signed matrices the off-diagonal integral could cancel across wavelengths without the supports being disjoint, whereas non-negative summands admit no cancellation. At the same time, a faithful round-trip requires each encoder row to overlap its own decoder column. Exact diagonality for all 𝑚 therefore forces a partition of the spectrum: each basis function owns a wavelength range, which is precisely binning.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
section: 3.4 The codec as a diagonal reduced matrix
text: Binning, however, caps accuracy: the comparison in Sec. 6.1 places every pure-binning variant at roughly 3× our error. The codec relaxes exact diagonality to diagonality in distribution: the training objective penalises off-diagonal leakage only on products of natural spectra, not for every conceivable 𝑚. This relaxation admits learned solutions that binning excludes, and the learning is where the accuracy is earned: in the same comparison, replacing the binaverage encoder with a learned one nearly halves the error of fixed boxes, and learning the decoder jointly nearly halves it again. The learned matrices keep nearly disjoint supports with small, deliberate overlaps (Supplemental Sec. 2). The codec is best understood as the distributionally-diagonal member of the reduced-matrix family that minimises rendered colour error.

Heterogeneous participating media. Per-voxel spectral data is encoded into the same 𝑘-dimensional latent space and stored as 𝐵 RGB-format grid volumes; each pass reads its triplet through the renderer's heterogeneous-medium machinery without modification. Linearity of the encoder makes this both practical and exact. Voxel spectra are typically blends of a few feature spectra, and encoding commutes with blending: the feature spectra are encoded once and their latent codes blended per voxel, so no per-voxel encoding is needed, and the renderer's volume filtering commutes with the encoding for the same reason (exactly so for trilinear and any nonnegative linear filter). Along a ray, the accumulated optical depth is a per-channel sum of voxel contributions, and sums are preserved exactly, as is rescaling by a scalar density field, which multiplies all channels by the same factor. Heterogeneity therefore introduces no approximation beyond the homogeneous regimes above: the deviation remains that of the per-channel exponential and the albedo ratio.
Per-class encoding parameters and renderer bindings are documented in Supplemental Sec. 6.

section: 5 Latent Upsampling for Legacy RGB Assets
text: While our codec compresses spectral inputs end-to-end, production pipelines hold large libraries of RGB textures, materials, and environment maps for which spectral data is unavailable. The obvious route for such assets is to uplift them with an existing RGB-to-spectrum method, for example Jakob and Hanika [2019], and encode the result. This composes two independent approximations: the uplift selects one metamer with no regard for the codec, and the encoder then compresses a spectrum that need not lie near its training distribution. We instead train lightweight networks that map the RGB input directly to a latent code. The prediction target is the code the codec itself would produce for the underlying spectrum, so the networks learn to land on codes that render accurately: on held-out data the composed route yields about 1 . 6× the colour error of direct prediction (the through-codec baseline rows of Tab. 5), while direct prediction stays close to the codec's own accuracy on ground-truth spectra. The upsamplers are a convenience bridge for RGB-only assets, not a spectral reconstruction method.

section: 5 Latent Upsampling for Legacy RGB Assets
text: Scope. Three boundaries delimit what these networks do. First, RGB-to-spectrum upsampling is one-to-many: a colour corresponds to many metamers, and a deterministic network selects a single one. Like all one-to-one upsamplers, ours does not address metamerism; when an asset's true spectrum differs from the selected metamer, relighting can diverge, and smooth selections are the safer choice. We therefore claim no recovery of true spectra: the target is a latent code that reproduces the asset's colour and renders robustly across illuminants. Second, unlike methods that enforce the input colour as a hard constraint, our round-trip is soft: Eq. (7) penalises but does not eliminate colour drift. The cost is small on reflectances (Supplemental Sec. 7) and is most visible under broadband illumination upsampling, where a hard-constrained uplift is close to exact by construction (Tab. 5); in exchange, the soft formulation is free to trade exact colour reproduction at one condition for rendering accuracy across conditions.

text: Third, scale equivariance is the correct prior for illumination, whose overall intensity is arbitrary, but for reflectance it forgoes the brightness information that recent uplift methods exploit to constrain the feasible metamer set; we accept this trade for a single shared mechanism across both asset types.

text: We evaluate the codec against spectral rendering as ground truth (Mitsuba 0.6 spectral build) and against standard RGB rendering as the practical baseline (the same Mitsuba 0.6 in RGB mode; the spectral build is never touched by our pipeline). We use 𝑘=6 (two RGB passes) throughout. All qualitative figures decode latents to spectra and CMF-integrate to sRGB. Sample budgets vary per scene class to balance Monte-Carlo noise against render time and are stated per figure; further tables and ablations are in the supplemental material.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Cornell-box evaluation under five illuminants. We first evaluate the codec at 𝑘=6 on a Cornell box containing diverse BRDFs and a ColorChecker chart, rendered under broadband, narrowband, structured, and multi-peaked illumination (Fig. 3; per-condition values in the figure). Materials and illuminants here are spectral ground truth encoded directly through the codec, with no upsampling involved. Across all five illuminants the latent pipeline reduces Δ𝐸2000 vs. spectral ground truth by 1 . 6 – 4 . 4× over standard RGB rendering; the advantage is largest under the structured red-dominant source narrow351 (0 . 86 vs. 3 . 82) and warm daylight (0 . 90 vs. 3 . 40). A 52-cell sweep over Gaussian-narrowband illuminants (13 centres × 4 FWHMs spanning the visible band) gives a mean per-cell codec advantage of 11 . 2× over RGB (Supplemental Sec. 5).

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Capacity and binning baselines. Since the learned decoder has nearly disjoint supports (Sec. 3.4), a natural question is whether plain wavelength binning at 𝑘=6 would suffice. It does not. Tab. 1 evaluates the full ladder on the same Cornell-box suite (illuminant SPDs in Fig. 4): three pure binning variants (bin-average encoder, box decoder, no training), the two half-learned bases (fixed decoder shape, trained encoder), and the jointly learned codec.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Averaged over the five illuminants, every binning variant, including bins placed at our own decoder's transitions, is about 3× less accurate than the learned codec and worse than plain RGB. The two narrowband columns expose why: binning accuracy depends on how the source's spectral structure falls relative to the fixed bin edges. The same adaptive bins score 1 . 33 when the 525 nm Gaussian lands near a bin centre and 6 . 69 on narrow 351 , whose red-dominant multi-lobed spectrum straddles several bin edges, and no placement resolves FL11's three emission peaks (5 . 0 – 5 . 6 vs. our 1 . 8). The codec is placement-robust (1 . 11 and 0 . 86) and remains the most accurate representation even in the binning-friendly 525 nm column. Nor is the decoder shape the whole contribution: on the same equal-width boxes, learning only the encoder cuts the average error nearly in half (4 . 35→2 . 36), and jointly learning the decoder nearly halves it again (→1 . 24).

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: The half-learned bases also expose a robustness failure the joint codec avoids: each is competitive on smooth broadband light but collapses on a different structured cell (boxes at 2 . 94 on the 525 nm source and 4 . 14 on FL11, Gaussians at 7 . 52 on FL11). The near-disjoint decoder is an outcome of the joint optimisation, not evidence that a box basis suffices. Fig. 5 shows the corresponding renders and error maps under FL11, the column where the differences are largest. PCA and NMF baselines and further per-illuminant breakdowns are in Supplemental Sec. 4.

On the Mitsuba matpreview test scene (Supplemental Sec. 2.4) under broadband and FL11 illumination, per-pixel error stabilises immediately: from direct lighting to one bounce the mean Δ𝐸 2000 rises by at most 0 . 02, then remains flat through 32 bounces (the maximum tested) at 0 . 91/1 . 62 (broadband) and 1 . 32/1 . 93 (FL11) for mean/p95. title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Approximation behaviour. Each per-channel regime of Sec. 4 replaces an exact spectral operation with a latent one. The bounds that follow are worst-case by construction: the stress chains iterate a single encoded spectrum, whereas real paths mix different surfaces whose encoding errors partially cancel, so rendered scene means sit at the foot of the curves. Even so, the deviations are bounded and slow-growing: repeated self-products of the same encoded spectrum stay below a Δ𝐸2000 of 5 through twelve surface crossings; Beer–Lambert transmittance error rises from the codec's product floor (0 . 96) to 1–6 at the reference depth; per-channel conductor Fresnel is nearly angle-independent below 60 ◦ , adding about two units at grazing incidence; and the single-scatter albedo ratio stays below 6 through twenty scattering orders for smooth subsurface materials, while saturated media use the factorised encoding. The characterisation curves, evaluated exactly as the pipeline operates and overlaid with the rendered scene means of this section, are in Supplemental Sec. 6.5.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: To verify that the codec deploys without renderer modification, we run it through four production frameworks: Blender Cycles (open-source path tracer; broadband and narrowband conditions), Autodesk Maya with Arnold (offline production), KeyShot (envmapdriven product visualisation), and Unreal Engine 5 (real-time rasteriser with Lumen global illumination). In each pipeline the latent code is treated as RGB material textures and light SPDs over two passes, and the decoder is a matrix multiply on the pass outputs.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Spectral ground truth is not natively available in these commercial pipelines, so we construct one per renderer: every material is uplifted to a spectrum with Jakob and Hanika [2019] (the reference is not built with our codec), light sources use their known SPDs, and each scene is rendered in 16 RGB-packed passes that reconstruct the full spectrum, stored as linear floating-point data with perrenderer response and exposure calibration (KeyShot and Cycles at 128 spp, Arnold at AA level 3, Unreal via the Movie Render Queue; configurations in Supplemental Sec. 9). Against this reference we evaluate three routes per scene (Figs. 10–13): the codec applied to the same spectral assets in two RGB passes, which isolates the codec's own error in each pipeline; the full RGB-asset route through our upsamplers, which adds the recovery cost; and the renderer's plain RGB baseline.

text:
Across the thirteen scene and lighting cases the codec's own error stays below 2 . 8 Δ𝐸 2000 in every renderer and lighting condition, the RGB-asset route adds a bounded upsampling premium, largest under Unreal's deliberately metameric lighting, and the plain RGB
baseline is the least accurate of the three in twelve of the thirteen cases. The exception is a nearly flat broadband source in Maya, smoother across the visible band than D65, under which all three routes fall within 2 Δ𝐸 2000 of the reference. Per-case means and 95th percentiles are in Supplemental Sec. 9. KeyShot is evaluated both under its environment map and under uniform-colour environment lights carrying the same known SPDs as the Maya cases; the RGB pipelines are the renderers' own linear outputs, brightness-matched to the reference.
A 120-frame animated sequence in Blender Cycles confirms temporal stability: no flicker or chromatic drift across either broadband or narrowband condition (per-renderer configurations and the supplemental video are in Supplemental Sec. 9).

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: We introduced a learned linear non-negative spectral codec that compresses spectra into 𝑘-dimensional spectral codes, exactly preserving scaling and addition and approximately preserving the perchannel product on which renderer shading operates. At equal 𝑘 , the learned basis is consistently more accurate than binning: on the Cornell box every binning variant is about 3× less accurate, learning the encoder over fixed boxes nearly halves the error, and jointly learning the decoder nearly halves it again (Sec. 6.1). At 𝑘=6 , two unmodified RGB passes through any path tracer reconstruct a spectral image to a mean Δ𝐸2000 between 0 . 7 and 2 . 7 (median 1 . 8) of the spectral ground truth across coloured glass, conductors, dipole and homogeneous subsurface scattering, and a per-voxel heterogeneous subsurface-scattering hand (Sec. 6.2); end-to-end wall-clock time is at near parity with Mitsuba 3's hero wavelength sampling on shading-bound scenes and about 1 . 8× on a traversal-bound interior (Sec. 6.5).

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Legacy RGB assets enter the same pipeline through small XYZ-conditioned upsampling networks that add a bounded premium over the no-upsampling reference (Sec. 6.3). Deployment is renderer-agnostic: we drove four production engines, Blender Cycles, Maya Arnold, KeyShot, and Unreal Engine 5, through the same two-pass interface unmodified, recovering colour information the RGB pipeline collapses. The renderer never changes; only the meaning of its three channels does. This is efficient spectral rendering without a spectral renderer. r.

title: Spectral Rendering Without a Spectral Renderer: Learned Spectral Codes for RGB Pipelines
text: Scope. The codec preserves only what reduces to per-channel arithmetic. Wavelength-shifting phenomena couple distinct wavelengths during transport and cannot be captured by a per-channel ⊙ regardless of 𝑘: fluorescence, phosphorescence, and the chromatic dispersion that arises from a wavelength-dependent index of refraction. BSDF non-linearities that escape per-channel arithmetic (e.g. a coated layer whose internal Fresnel contains exp(−𝜎 𝑑) along a wavelength-dependent path) similarly fall outside the supported regime; Sec. 4 enumerates the cases that are inside it. Layered materials, whose cross-layer coupling is non-linear in the spectra, are a natural target for future work under the same constraint. Residual error is largest under extremely peaked illuminants and after many indirect interactions, but Sec. 6.2 shows it stabilises with bounce count rather than diverging. The advantage is concentrated where an RGB pipeline discards spectral information. On spectrally bland media and under smooth broadband light the RGB baseline loses little, and the codec's own reconstruction floor of one to two Δ𝐸2000
